speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, enhance measures to address the increasing misuse of technology to produce and circulate abusive materials.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, enhance protection for minors and vulnerable victims.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fourth, better protect public servants and public service workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Fifth, ensure adequate penalties for older youth offenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann) (for the Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sixth, recalibrate the requirements on workers and dealers of precious metals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members may also access these materials through the MP@SGPARL app.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They constitute 60% of all reported crimes, and the losses are more than three and a half times the cost of building Woodlands Health Campus.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA has been working with other agencies and the private sector on measures to counter the scourge of scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Earlier this year, Dr Tan Wu Meng suggested in this House that MHA also consider introducing caning for scams, to better deter and punish those who commit scams or facilitate the commission of scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have reviewed the suggestion and agree with it.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members may refer to Part A of the Annex for the proposed amendments.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also introduce discretionary caning in section 420 of the Penal Code for serious cases of cheating.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will take an equally firm stance against scam syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These syndicates mobilise significant resources to conduct and profit from scams and have the highest level of culpability.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Beyond dealing with scammers and scam syndicates, another key strategy is to deny them the tools that enable them to conduct scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These scam enablers include SIM cards, Singpass credentials and payment accounts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Crippling the supply of scam enablers would significantly increase the difficulty for scammers to successfully conduct or profit from scams in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will therefore introduce discretionary caning for those who facilitate scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These are offenders who either knew or had reasonable grounds to believe that the scam enabler they provide, would be used in the commission of, or would be used in the facilitation of, a crime.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clauses 10, 11, 19, 20 and 30 to 34 of the Bill introduce discretionary caning for certain offences under the Miscellaneous Offences (Public Order and Nuisance) Act, the Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes (Confiscation of Benefits) Act, and the Computer Misuse Act, in this regard.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For upstream enablers such as Singpass credentials and SIM cards, discretionary caning will broadly apply to two categories of cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The first category is where the offender intended or knew, depending on the offence, that the enabler would be used to commit or facilitate the commission of a scam.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The second category covers cases where the enabler is actually used to commit or facilitate the commission of a scam, even if the offender did not intend or know this.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For the second category of offenders, discretionary caning will apply if the offender fails to prove that he or she had taken reasonable steps to ensure that the enabler would not be used to commit or to facilitate the commission of a scam.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For downstream enablers such as payment accounts, discretionary caning will apply if the criminal proceeds laundered involve benefits from a scam and the offender had failed to take reasonable steps to ensure that the account is not used to launder scam proceeds.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The existing offences do not penalise genuine victims in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Ministry will continue monitoring the scams situation closely and will further increase our penalties if needed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In Mandarin):   The Government continues to place strong emphasis on combating scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While these numbers have decreased compared with the first half of 2024, they are still significant.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In this Bill, we are proposing to introduce mandatory caning for scammers, as well as members and recruiters of scam syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also introduce discretionary caning for those who facilitate scams through providing enablers, such as their Singpass credentials, SIM cards or bank accounts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If we can deny scammers access to such enablers, it will be much more difficult for them to carry out successful scams and we can better protect Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: (In English): Sir, even as we introduce caning for scams, we also intend to recalibrate the use of caning in other offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, there are 96 offences that attract discretionary caning and 65 which attract mandatory caning.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: My Ministry has conducted a review, to ensure that caning is only applied where there is a need.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As Members can see from Part B of the Annex, we are proposing to amend eight provisions to remove caning entirely and in the case of vandalism, to remove caning for a subset of the offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As our societal context and crime situation have evolved, caning may no longer be necessary in some offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These are generally offences that do not involve intentional harm to a person nor cause significant harm to the public and for which we assess that the other penalties are adequate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clauses 41, 61, 67 and 69 to 76 of the Bill make the necessary amendments.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For 15 provisions reflected in Part C of the Annex, we propose to give the Courts the discretion to decide whether to impose caning, rather than to require caning in all cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These are given effect by clauses 15 to 17, 40, 54 to 60, 62, 65, 66 and 72 to 74 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For avoidance of doubt, more serious cases should still result in caning, even as we make these amendments to change mandatory caning to discretionary caning.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The latter category includes private property that is of national, cultural or religious significance and any other private property that the Minister may prescribe – in short, primarily property that has public significance or serves a public function.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For these vandalism offences, we will leave it to the Court to decide whether caning should be imposed on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This approach maintains a firm stance against vandalism generally, while allowing the punishment to be calibrated based on the facts of each case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Court may consider factors like the extent of property damage, the vandal's motivations, the degree of premeditation, and the impact on public services and functions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Similarly, in other offences which only involve preparatory acts or do not require an element of harm to be present before the offence is made out, we have assessed that discretionary caning is adequate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Courts can still impose caning in serious cases where real harm results or there are other aggravating factors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This includes certain offences under the Corrosive, Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act, as well as attempted robbery and making preparation for gang-robbery under sections 393 and 399 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The amendments do not signal any softening in our stance against crime.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The large majority of offences which attract caning today, including serious sexual and violence offences, will continue to attract caning as a punishment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, we are introducing amendments to deal with large-scale circulation of obscene objects, which include sexual images or videos.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members will recall the case of the chat group SG Nasi Lemak, in which over 44,000 members circulated and shared obscene materials involving women and girls.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government's view is that the current penalties are not adequate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Technology allows obscene materials to be shared with tens of thousands of recipients, through a single key stroke.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We cannot begin to imagine the distress suffered by a young girl whose images are sent to thousands of prying eyes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And because these materials can be sent to so many people, it is impossible to take them out of circulation entirely.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They will always be lurking somewhere, threatening to resurface.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These victims may never have peace of mind again.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This threshold takes reference from other provisions where the involvement of 10 or more persons introduces a public dimension.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, under the Societies Act, the threshold size of a group that must be registered as a society is 10 persons.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The maximum imprisonment term for such offences will be increased from three months to two years.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These enhanced penalties will also apply to cumulative transmissions to 10 or more persons in total, to close the potential loophole of accused persons sending separate messages to single individuals, but to a large number of individuals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In addition, clause 43 of the Bill introduces a new offence to target those who set up or manage online locations where obscene materials are circulated, including administrators of chat groups or channels, blogs, or accounts on video-sharing platforms.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The offence is scoped to offenders who intend that the online location be used to circulate obscene materials.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It will not cover, for example, platforms whose online locations are used in this way contrary to their original intent or administrators whose chat groups are spammed by bad actors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, we also intend to deal with the problem of images and videos generated by the use of artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: By virtue of section 377BE(5) of the Penal Code, our criminal laws already cover sexually explicit deepfakes, where an image or recording is altered to depict the victim.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It is already an offence to possess or gain access to, or to distribute or threaten to distribute such sexual deepfakes without consent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, generative AI now makes it possible to generate entirely synthetic images or videos of a person, without making use of a pre-existing image or recording.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clauses 50(a) and (b) of the Bill update the relevant provision to get ahead of this development.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clause 49(d) makes clear that it is an offence to produce any intimate image without consent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, such offenders would already be liable for the offence of possessing or gaining access to an intimate image, but we want to make criminal liability clearer as far as production of the intimate image is concerned.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clause 50(c) makes explicit what has always been our intent that for the offence of threatening to distribute an intimate image, it is not necessary to prove that the intimate image exists.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such threats can cause serious harm even if the intimate image does not exist, especially now that it is easier to generate such images using AI.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: When the relevant offences were introduced in 2019, it was always the Government's intention to criminalise realistic computer-generated child abuse material, even if the material depicts a fictional child.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The offences should not require proof that an actual child was involved, for example, that an image of an actual child was used as part of the training data for the AI used to generate the material.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is both to reduce the roadblocks to enforcement and to reduce the supply of such materials, which contributes to a vicious cycle of abuse.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clause 53 of the Bill amends the relevant definitions to put these points beyond doubt.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This will also bring us in line with the United Nations' Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child on the Sale of Children, Child Prostitution and Child Pornography.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, we propose to strengthen the sexual grooming offences under sections 376E and 376EA of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, the offences generally only apply if the groomer and victim meet or intend to meet in Singapore for the sexual acts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There have, however, been cases where sexual grooming charges could not be preferred because the sexual acts were done or intended to be done overseas.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clauses 47 and 48 of the Bill will amend the sexual grooming offences so that they will also apply to sexual acts intended to be done overseas, as long as the acts would constitute an offence if done in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To prevent overreach, this will only apply where either the groomer or victim travels from a location in Singapore to meet overseas.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The amendments also increase the penalties for sexual grooming offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are introducing life imprisonment because there is strong public interest to deter abuse of vulnerable persons.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Often, they are voiceless, they cannot protect themselves, and they depend on others for even their basic needs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And so, when they are abused to the point of death, it is especially heinous and must be met with the full force of the law.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Take the tragic case of the young boy who was scalded to death by his parents a few years ago.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In 2022, his mother was convicted of murder while his father was convicted of voluntarily causing grievous hurt by means of a heated substance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Although the father's charge was not for causing death but only endangering life, the Court of Appeal found that life imprisonment was justified given the cruelty and severity of the abuse.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Moving forward, similar cases may be prosecuted under sections 304B and 304C of the Penal Code instead as these provisions were specifically introduced to overcome certain hurdles in prosecuting cases of fatal abuse.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The amendments will ensure that life imprisonment will be available as a sentencing option in such cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The fourth category of amendments addresses protections for public servants and public service workers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Many public servants and public service workers are at risk of being doxed in the course of performing their duties, that is, having their identity information published with the intent to cause harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Doxxing can impede or deter them from discharging their duties objectively and impartially, and when accompanied by falsehoods, can also undermine public confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, we will strengthen the protections for public servants and public service workers under section 6 of the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, this offence requires proof that the victim actually suffered harm, alarm or distress.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: All harassment of public servants or public service workers in the line of duty is unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For the purposes of securing a conviction, it should not matter whether or to what degree the victim experienced harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The extent of harm experienced by the victim should, of course, still be a factor for sentencing.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such conduct is especially harmful because not only are the individual public servants adversely affected, but trust in our public institutions is undermined.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Section 7 of the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) today already criminalises the publishing of a falsehood if that specific falsehood diminishes public confidence, but this new offence will not have that requirement of needing to show diminution of public confidence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To be clear, neither of these amendments prevents members of the public from expressing legitimate feedback or criticism, including publicly.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such feedback, expressed constructively and through the appropriate channels, can help us improve our service delivery and staff training.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There will also not be any offence disclosed if the feedback is based on genuinely mistaken facts, since the offence requires that the person know or have reason to believe that a statement of fact is false.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The policy intent, however, was to ensure that if youth offenders between the ages of 16 and 18 commit serious offences or repeat offences, their cases could be transferred out of the Youth Court to the High Court and State Courts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In those cases, it was always intended that the High Court and State Courts will continue to have the full suite of powers to deal with the offenders.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, when preparing to operationalise the CYPA amendments, we identified certain provisions in the earlier round of amendments which are not fully aligned with the policy intent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Clauses 3 to 7, and 23 of the Bill straighten out these provisions and ensure that the policy intent is given its full effect.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To be clear, the amendments will not require the Court to impose these penalties, nor otherwise limit the Court's discretion in sentencing.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Court can still, upon a close examination of the facts, impose a rehabilitative sentence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The final set of amendments, Sir, in clauses 26 to 28 of the Bill pertains to workers and dealers of precious metals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This will give the Police more time to trace and recover stolen goods.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Stolen goods usually come from a customer, rather than from another dealer.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The overall intent of the amendments is to improve law enforcement's ability to trace stolen goods and the criminals, while minimising the burden on businesses in a risk-calibrated manner.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They will help MHA carry out our mission of keeping Singapore safe and secure more effectively.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We seek the support of Members for the amendments.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: First, the amendments regarding the large-scale electronic circulation of obscene objects; and second, the amendments regarding scams and scam-related offences.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: First, on the large-scale electronic circulation of obscene objects.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I fully agree with and applaud the Government for creating a new offence to target administrators who set up or manage online locations to facilitate the large-scale circulation of obscene material.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I believe this will allow the Government to better go after the source of the problem and deal with the problem at its source and hopefully, deter the problem at its source as well.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I also agree with the Government that such administrators who set up or manage online locations to facilitate the large-scale circulation of obscene material have a higher level of culpability compared to members of the online location who share obscene content.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But I wish to suggest even stiffer penalties for such administrators.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We can and should go further, to introduce discretionary caning for administrators of online locations circulating obscene material, to bring the penalties for such offences in line with those for assault or use of criminal force to a person with the intent to outrage modesty, under section 354 of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Because the criminal force inflicted through electronic means by administrators of online locations on their victims is certainly no less severe than the criminal force inflicted in person by a physical perpetrator.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And many a times, the criminal force inflicted is probably even more severe, due to the multiplicity and simultaneity of the outrage on modesty made possible by electronic means to assault a victim at scale and at speed.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Discretionary caning for administrators of online locations circulating obscene material is, therefore, proportionate and fits the crime.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Given the prevalence and extreme ease to become an administrator of such online locations, discretionary caning is also needed as a deterrent.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Therefore, the nature of the offence of administering online locations to circulate obscene materials fits both the functions of proportionality and deterrence that judicial caning today serves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Scams are operated in a way, basically, like drugs are.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Scams are perpetrated by organised crime syndicates, like drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And scams are masterminded and commandeered remotely, from overseas, with the most downstream part of the production chain of criminal activities sited onshore, in Singapore – just like drugs are.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Scams cause immense harm to society, just like drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: If drugs destroy lives, scams destroy life savings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And because scammers often impersonate Government agencies, scams can also erode the trust of our society at-large, in our key institutions, like the Police, the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, and so on.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, scams do not just affect victims, they impact the whole of society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Our key institutions have to react, put up defences and these defences come at a cost.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, scams extract a cost on the whole of our society, every day.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Scams cause immense harm to society, just like drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, our criminal laws should deal with scams just like they deal with drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I suggest that penalties for scams and scam-related offences should be brought more in line with those for drug-related offences, at three levels.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In other words, the masterminds, the key operators, the most culpable, those at the highest level in the chain.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Scammers manufacture schemes on an industrial level to cheat victims of their life savings.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: In my mind, scammers are, therefore, no less harmful to our society than manufacturers of controlled Class A drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I will stop short of calling for capital punishment for the most egregious scammers, which should be in line with the penalty for manufacturers of specific Class A drugs, like morphine, cocaine and methamphetamine.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: We know the scammers, masterminds and key operators, are mostly based overseas; just like the masterminds and key manufacturers of illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But having very stiff penalties for scammers is an important and necessary marker, in my view.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Many of these members and recruiters of scam syndicates are based in, or come through, Singapore, unlike the scammers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: If scammers are as harmful to our society as manufacturers of Class A drugs, in my mind, scam syndicate members and recruiters are as harmful as traffickers of Class A drugs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The amendments before us today introduce, again, mandatory caning for such scam syndicate members and recruiters, minimum six strokes.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: To my mind, these are the lowest levels of the scam crime production chain.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Yes, they do harm, they have culpability, but they are the lowest levels.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to speak today on two matters that I find most significant: first, on tackling scams; second, on the reduction in the use of caning for other offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also have some queries on the new offence of doxxing of public servants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My party colleague, Member Fadli Fawzi, will speak later on related issues and other aspects of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is clear that despite significant efforts poured into anti-scam measures, Singaporeans are still falling prey to scams and losing significant sums.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Banks have made efforts to strengthen digital banking to detect and delay unusual transactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Public education has intensified: there is now even an anti-scam warning on the Parliament website.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Scam organisations are brilliant at social engineering and tailoring their ruses to suit the intended victim.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In one case I came across, the scammers even coached the victim as to what to tell Police if she was questioned, which she dutifully complied with, as if under some sort of spell.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, we are dealing with highly sophisticated operators.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Although there are existing laws to cover these situations, the new provisions create new specific offences or enhance the punishment if they are committed through scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How effective the provisions will be will depend on how tightly they can be enforced – no point having strict laws if offenders are not pursued.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is also likely that even if persons are caught, offender displacement will occur – meaning that there will be no shortage of persons willing to replace them, if the rewards are lucrative enough.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For organised scams, effective enforcement will require agencies across borders to share information and conduct joint operations as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At this point, it is not clear to me how committed every government in Southeast Asia is towards combatting scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It was further reported that Cambodian police found evidence of the involvement of other suspects and this evidence formed the basis for the Singapore Police Force (SPF) to issue INTERPOL Red Notices against them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the handling of this case so far shows strong cross-border cooperation, I wonder if such extensive cooperation happens on a regular basis.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, does the Ministry expect in future to utilise the expanded powers under the Extradition Act to request the Association for Southeast Asian Nation (ASEAN) neighbours to hand over such suspects to Singapore through extradition?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To respond to this, some governments are using other tools besides the criminal law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two months ago, the American Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, issued a statement highlighting that "criminal actors across Southeast Asia" had, and I quote, "increasingly exploited the vulnerabilities of Americans online", resulting in an estimated loss of US$10 billion last year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He announced that the American government would impose sanctions on various persons and entities involved in running a scam centre in Myanmar and forced labour compounds in Cambodia.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He opined that the sanctions would have the effect of disrupting the ability of the criminal networks to perpetuate their fraudulent and abusive activities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, it would be useful to know to what extent the Singapore Government will also consider other tools outside the criminal law to disrupt such organised scam groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill also introduces caning as an additional option in scam cases involving the misuse of Singpass credentials under the Computer Misuse Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The same is being done under the Miscellaneous Offences Act for scams involving the misuse of SIM cards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for cheating under the Penal Code, there will be mandatory caning if done through remote communications, such as the Internet, telephone or electronic or other technology.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given the tremendous material loss and psychological harm caused to scam victims, I have little sympathy for those who perpetrate these cruel acts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, the sentence of caning is a harsh punishment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it is a legacy of our colonial past, it is a punishment where the state inflicts violence and physical pain on a prisoner.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From reported accounts of some who underwent the punishment, caning led them to bleed and by some accounts, to suffer such pain that it led them to go into a state of shock.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that light, could the Ministry elaborate on why it has assessed that caning will be effective to reduce scam activity?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Did the Ministry consider alternatives, such as providing for longer jail terms and heavier fines?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my second point which is related.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I strongly welcome the reduction in the use of caning for other offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In its press release on 14 October, the Ministry stated that it made these moves considering factors such as whether the offences were still of significant public concern and whether other punishments sufficed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This review – to remove unnecessary punishments – brings important balance to this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The amendments proposed to the Vandalism Act are particularly significant and welcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, caning will exist as an option for the Court, in cases where the vandalism is deemed more serious.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Social conditions change over time, and our laws should be fit for purpose.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is currently on a short list of about 30 countries that still have corporal punishment on its criminal statutes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we must decide for ourselves what is appropriate for our criminal justice system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I believe Singaporeans will support a criminal justice system that is effective and at the same time, humane.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the section will apply to protect public servants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As to who would be considered a public servant, the proposed definition refers to the definition of public servant in the Penal Code, as well as any person who, under other written laws, is deemed a public servant for the purposes of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If so, would someone holding a political position, such as a Minister or Member of Parliament (MP), be covered under the section?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, the section prohibits the publication of identity information, not just about the public servant but also a "related person".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The definition of "related person" is stated as "another person about whose safety or well-being the (public servant) would reasonably be expected to be seriously concerned".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This definition is inexact and potentially includes almost everyone, including family members, colleagues and acquaintances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the intended ambit of the definition of "related person"?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is an illustration clarifying that the doxxing offence would be made out where the false statement and the identity information were carried in two separate online posts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, this illustration is found in the Explanatory Statement to the Bill and is not part of the text of the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would seem to me to be more appropriate to carry the illustration upfront in the law itself, to make it clearly visible to anyone looking up the law in the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, having it in the Explanatory Statement makes it harder to locate and may lead to unnecessary arguments down the road.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill confronts us with decisions about the use of caning as a judicial punishment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In view of the devastating harms scammers have caused and continue to cause to Singaporean families, I believe the public supports the amendments regarding scam offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, there is a concerted effort in the Bill to remove or reduce the use of caning for various other offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a move I fully endorse, as we work to scope our criminal laws more tightly and appropriately.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I applaud the Ministry's move to update sexual offences to protect our people, especially the young and the vulnerable, in an ever-evolving digital landscape.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The amendments proposed have been designed to be able to factor in future developments and trends in technology and social media.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These amendments bring us in line with international standards and are crucial to allow us to respond to cases like the SG Nasi Lemak Telegram group, which saw thousands exposed to such harmful material.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Importantly, the amendments make it clear that consensual and private sharing of intimate images between adults will not be criminalised, reaffirming the law's focus on protecting, but not policing citizens' private lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this is the case, I hope that people continue to be careful about who they share their intimate content with, especially in the face of potential love scams or even blackmail, amongst other possibilities for abuse or misuse.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also like to suggest that such potential harms are addressed in sex education classes in schools.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These images, though not constructed from real photographs, are equally harmful and can devastate reputations and cause emotional damage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The law must remain ahead of technology and this amendment sends a strong deterrent message to would-be offenders that "virtual" crimes are, in fact, very real, with equally real and painful penalties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would also reinforce what our society considers to be obscene.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While these are laudable steps, I would urge the Government to pay closer attention to bullying cases, in situations where it could entail the distribution of intimate images of minors, which can be weaponised as a form of sexualised bullying.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While legal deterrence is very important, the penalties imposed on the perpetrators are by themselves not able to help support the recovery of the victims or to cope with the aftermath of the bullying attacks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Therefore, I hope that there will be clear guidelines and robust victim support systems to protect the vulnerable young victims.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill introduces stronger measures to deter harassment, doxxing and the making of false allegations against public servants, recognising the negative impact these acts have on public officers and, by extension, public confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: No longer must the victim prove harassment, alarm or distress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Intent to harass is enough and this is a much needed strengthening of deterrence without placing undue burden on the doxxing victim to prove that they had suffered.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This recognises that false narratives can rapidly undermine confidence in public institutions and make it difficult for public servants to perform their jobs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the past five years, scams have shattered lives and torn families apart, with Singaporeans losing billions of dollars.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some victims feel so desperate that they resort to tragic ends.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Families are broken by trust betrayed, and savings painstakingly built over lifetimes are wiped out in a moment.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deterrence must be robust and, as past experience with loan shark harassment shows, caning is effective in reducing recalcitrant crime.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the punishment is severe, the harm caused to victims, whose lives are often ruined, justifies the tough response.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, cross-border cooperation is still very important in the enforcement of these laws, in order to bring the criminals to justice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mandatory caning for scammers and syndicate members, and discretionary caning for so-called "mules" will send an unequivocal signal: Singapore will not tolerate those who prey on our people, be it from behind a keyboard or through sophisticated networks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deterrence must be robust and past experience with loan shark harassment shows – caning is effective in reducing recalcitrant crime.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While the punishment is severe, the harm caused to victims – whose lives are often ruined – justifies the tough response.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, cross-border cooperation is still very important in the enforcement of these laws, in order to bring the criminals to justice.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the amendments before us today make our laws more relevant, responsive and robust in the face of new threats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support the Bill, even as I urge for continued vigilance, including in victim support, clarity for bullying cases and stronger protection for public servants, in the age of ease of doxxing.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am supportive of the Bill's intentions, especially the changes which allow us to keep pace with the ever-evolving nature of crimes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill addresses important lacunae in the law that have emerged as a result of technological advances, some of which may have extra territorial implications.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The Bill also affords public servants better protections from harassment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As an MP overseeing the running of a Town Council, I fully understand the need for these amendments.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I have seen how our hardworking Town Council staff have been unfairly targeted with their names and identities spread around by some unhappy residents.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: On one hand, caning has been introduced for certain categories of scam- and fraud-related offences.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, caning has been removed or made discretionary for other offences, such as specific vandalism offences.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I mentioned the Vandalism Act, in particular, because there were some disquiet, both in public and in Parliament, when caning was first mooted as a penalty.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For instance, the Vandalism Act has been described by legal academic Jothie Rajah as a significant departure from penal practises in prescribing a violent punishment for a property offence when it was introduced in 1966.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is worth noting that the then-Law Minister EW Barker recognised the unique nature of Singapore's caning policy on vandalism.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: He said, "At the outset, it must be considered that the present day penological trends are against the infliction of caning as punishment, and that legal opinion is, in general, against the imposition of corporal punishment in cases not involving violence or brutality." In the same debate, then-People's Action Party (PAP) backbencher, Mr Tang See Chim, also warned, and here I am quoting him, "That the severity of the punishment may not, in fact, necessarily be a deterrent.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The way to deter any crime, I submit, is to impress on the wrongdoer the certainty of his being found out if he commits one." Sir, we seem to have come full circle from 1966.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Now, we are about to cease mandatory caning as punishment for vandalism.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, however, we are introducing corporal punishment for a new class of offences related to frauds and scams.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It goes without saying that we need to protect Singaporeans from scammers.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Their modus operandi grows ever more sophisticated and multifarious, and it can seem as though we are trying to fight a hydra.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Of course, we would want to use all the weapons we have at our disposal to confront this hydra-headed challenge.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As we consider caning as punishment against scammers, I do believe the points raised in the debate on the Vandalism Act in 1966 can still be relevant.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In particular, they were concerned about whether caning is an appropriate deterrence against crime.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I do not wish to understate the severity of the monetary losses as a result of scams: it can run up to life-changing amounts or even the entirety of an elderly person's retirement funds.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Many of us in the House, myself included, will have encountered scam victims seeking assistance at our meet-the-people sessions.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The scale of their losses can be heartbreaking.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How should we fight the hydra of these scam networks?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Would caning be effective and is it appropriate?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: As many of us are aware, scams are now increasingly being perpetrated by organised crime networks.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: It is quite likely that the ringleaders would be cocooned safely somewhere, far from Singapore, in countries that may not have extradition treaties with us.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, the lower-level operatives are the ones on the frontlines and liable to be caught.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Would caning the latter group of individuals cause a dent on their criminal operations?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Furthermore, would introducing the prospect of being caned substantially change the calculus for the ringleaders?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: From the perspective of disrupting these scam operations, it may actually make more of a difference if we strengthen cross-border law enforcement cooperation and extradition arrangements.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge that this is being done by the Government.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My point, however, is that we can better deter the ringleaders by increasing the likelihood of them being caught, rather than the prospect of more severe punishment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Another possibility is to offer leniency to lower-level operatives who assist the authorities in dismantling these crime networks.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Many of these lower-level operatives, including the mules, may be unwilling participants who have been, themselves, tricked into working for these criminal networks.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am aware of the operational details of something like a victim restitution fund, would have to be worked out carefully.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, unlike caning, this offers a more tangible benefit to the victims.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I fervently believe that scam victims deserve justice for the psychological and material losses they have to endure.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I can also understand the appeal of bringing the full force of the law onto these scammers who have left so much misery and pain in their wake.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, the law is not a blunt instrument, but something to be used with precision.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our laws must keep pace with the way harm is spread today through closed chats, fast moving platforms and AI tools that can humiliate in seconds.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill makes targeted amendments across several key acts, including the Penal Code, Criminal Procedure Code, Computer Misuse Act, Corruption, Drug Trafficking and Other Serious Crimes Act, and the Miscellaneous Offences Act.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, these changes modernise our criminal laws, ensuring firm deterrence, comprehensive protection and a justice system that remains fair and trusted.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Given the breadth of this Bill, I will focus my remarks on two key areas.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, the measures to deter scams and technology-enabled crimes, particularly, how they protect vulnerable residents, including seniors in older estates, such as mine in Kolam Ayer, and across the Jalan Besar group representation constituency (GRC).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, the protection of our frontline public service officers, our teachers, our healthcare workers, our Home Team officers, among others who serve with dedication, but are increasingly vulnerable to online harassments and false allegations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a labour MP, I will also touch on how these changes strengthen workplace protection and mental well-being for those who serve the public every day.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They prey on trust, create financial pain and leave victims, especially seniors, feeling ashamed or helpless.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In Kolam Ayer and across Jalan Besar, I have met elderly residents who have fallen prey to scams.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some were tricked into disclosing their bank details, others believed they were helping a family member in distress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For many, it was their life's saving, painstakingly build over decades, that vanish in mere minutes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They enable syndicates to prey on the unsuspecting and amplify harm across the community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is appropriate because behind every scammer or mule stands a victim who loses not just money, but confidence and dignity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, deterrence must be matched with precision and prevention.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To that end, I seek two clarifications from the Ministry.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For example, when they procure SIMs, multi-wallet control, profit shares and script coaching, so that the Courts can distinguish mastermind from the low-level participants.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask this because clearer distinctions help to ensure that penalties fall proportionately on those who profit most, while preventing unfair outcomes for those who have limited involvement.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Will there be positive checklists defining what counts as reasonable steps for first-time offenders or mules?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will prevent sham compliance and give fair notice to those tempted by easy money.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask this because clear guidance can deter borderline cases before they can actually occur, especially among the young or financially desperate individuals who may not grasp the full consequence of aiding a scam.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our laws are strongest when our people are informed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors and low-income residents remain vulnerable to scams because of their limited digital literacy.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I hope with this enforcement, we continue to be complemented by sustained public education through our digital ambassadors, our community volunteers, so that every resident can navigate the digital world with confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Strong deterrent must be matched by proactive education so that no Singaporean feels unprotected in this increasingly digital landscape.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My second point, Sir, is on protecting frontline public service officers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In recent years, we have seen public officers unfairly targeted online, their names and photos circulated with false claims.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At Tan Tock Seng Hospital, a patient uploaded a police report online and falsely named a doctor as being involved in an alleged mistreatment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The hospital later clarified that the named doctor was not involved, but by then, the harm to his reputation and peace of mind was already done.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Ministry of Education has also acknowledged that educators and even students, had been doxed and attacked online, following the Sengkang Green Primary School incident.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Teachers, who dedicate their life nurturing our children, should never have to fear harassment simply for doing their jobs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our Home Team officers, who enforce laws and respond to emergencies, have at times, been filmed, misrepresented and vilified online, such as the 2021 Yishun case, where a video falsely accused Police Officers of bullying an elderly woman.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Investigations later showed that the Police were actually helping the woman, not harassing her, and a POFMA correction was issued.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This shifts the focus where it belongs on the offenders' intent, not the victim's reaction.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, three clarifications may help strengthen this protection further.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask this because such tongue-in-cheek posts can still mislead the public and incite, ridicule or harass our officers who are carrying out their duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A short policy note would be helpful to agencies, employers and even unions, who can help to apply the law consistently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask this because operational clarity prevents hesitation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Agencies and unions must know which legal route to take swiftly to safeguard their officers and restore public confidence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask this because similarly, these workers will face some public exposure – same risk as civil servants – yet they lack the institutional protection or recourse channels available to them.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As a labour MP, I am heartened that this Bill recognises both public servants and public service workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The latter includes nurses, our Town Council staff and contract personnel who keep Singapore running every day.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their service deserves the same protection and respect.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Unions, such as the Healthcare Services Employees Union and the Singapore Teachers' Union, have long advocated these protections, standing beside our workers who face harassment or stigma during the course of duty.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must ensure that every person who serves the public, regardless of employer, can do so safely and with dignity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, this Bill strengthens justice and safety in our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It does not merely punish the perpetrators; it also protects those who are vulnerable and safeguards the dignity of public officers who have shown total dedication in performing their duty.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Through these amendments, we enhance penalties for cyber scams, extend protection to public officers and frontline workers, and ensure that our laws remain relevant in this digital era.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In short, justice is not just about meting out punishment – it is about preserving trust, safety and humanity. : Mr Speaker, this Bill represents an important step in strengthening both justice and trust.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By deterring scams, we protect our seniors, our workers and our families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By protecting our officers and public service workers, we safeguard those who uphold the values of duty, care and compassion.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Good law leaves no easy exits for bad actors and gives confidence to those who protect us.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: With this Bill, we will send a clear signal that Singapore stands firm against harm and stands with those who protect and serve our people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given its breadth, I will focus my remarks on three areas: one, tackling global scams and online crimes while protecting innovation; two, a calibrated approach to accountability for 14-to-17-year-olds; and three, improving proportionality by resolving the inflexibility of mandatory caning.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I support forward-looking legislation that go after the operators – scam networks, credential abuse, deepfakes, child sexual abuse material (CSAM) creators – without impeding technological progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Indeed, the impact of such crimes is immense.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Victims, like many of my fellow Members have mentioned, are disproportionately elderly, vulnerable or desperate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many lose their life savings and suffer deep hardship.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But when a forest fire breaks out, we do not try to stop the wind; we go after the arsonists of that forest fire.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It focuses on those who exploit technology for harm – organised crime networks, scam operators and credential traffickers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Criminalising the misuse of another's identity or SIM registration cuts off the pathways in which scams spread.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Each stolen credential is a spark, each mule account, a dry branch.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, this Bill builds the firebreaks we need while keeping the wind free so that legitimate innovation can grow.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This Bill implements and clarifies the 2019 Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA) changes to treat ages 14 to below 18 as young persons and expands Youth Court coverage while preserving the ability to transmit serious or repeat cases to the State Courts or the High Court, so that adequate penalties can be imposed where warranted.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many teenagers today are better informed and more mature, compared to youths decades ago.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For very serious crimes, we should hold them responsible.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But maturity is a continuum; one does not gain wisdom and fortitude at a precise birthday.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Lastly, I welcome the calibrated caning penalties for 22 offences while introducing caning as a penalty for scamming.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Today, multiple statutes impose minimum strokes and leave the Court with no room to calibrate punishment.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is a one-size-fits-all penalties for those laws.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The new flexibility from this Bill for 22 offences provides judicial discretion to weigh mitigation factors on a case-by-case basis, for example, first-offender status, coercion or duress, genuine remorse, or early plea.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is the law taking full account of both harm and human circumstances.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: At the same time, given the severe impact of scamming, I fully support the inclusion of caning penalties for scamming crimes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It also aligns accountability with maturity, and it restores judicial discretion when it is due.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It protects our people and our progress while keeping justice fair and firm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It strengthens our laws against scams, amends sexual offences, raises penalties for causing or allowing fatal abuse to vulnerable victims, revises sentencing for young offenders and updates older provisions to fit today's realities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At its core, it defines new offences, allowing caning for some scam-related crimes, removes caning from others, and refines how we deal with youths and vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this response, I will focus on deterring scams through tougher and more targeted measures.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In Clementi, I have walked the ground and sought help for my residents who fell into victims of scams.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Their stories are heartbreaking and even more painful when I learnt how their families are affected.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I would like to highlight four clarifications and considerations.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The first is on discretionary caning and proportionality.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, scams can wipe out the life savings of many and shatter families.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, I would like to better understand how the upper limit of 12 strokes was set.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, was the upper limit of 12 strokes benchmarked against other offences with similar harm and culpability?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Were the existing caning-eligible offences considered and used as comparisons when setting this upper limit and if so, what was the principle for alignment?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to hear earlier that the upper limit has room for review.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: On this note, we should be clear what caning is not.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This brings me to my second point on the economics of deterrence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As someone who had spent years teaching economics, I tend to think of deterrence as a simple equation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Does the expected cost outweigh the expected benefit?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, the expected cost of committing a crime depends on three things.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One, severity – how harsh that punishment is.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Two, certainty – how likely you are to be caught and punished.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And three, speed – how fast the punishment happens.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In short, deterrence, in my view, mentions three things: severity, certainty and speed.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because if scammers believe they never will, or are unlikely to be caught, perhaps because they are hiding behind a fake or an anonymous account, or operate outside of Singapore, then harsher penalties might not make much of a difference.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, beyond raising penalties, we should raise the certainty, visibility and speed of enforcement and punishment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: At the end of the day, we measure what is important to us.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, the Government should consider publishing regular updates on scam activities – how many were reported, caught, and continue amplifying public communications.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because this sends a clear signal that Singapore does not just punish harshly, but we also catch swiftly, in this context of scam activities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many scams that hit Singapore are not run from here.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The threat of caning here may not deter someone who sits overseas or never plans to set foot in Singapore.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The answer then, in my view, has to be stronger and faster cross-border cooperation, coordination and enforcement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore already works with partners within ASEAN, INTERPOL and other countries.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My point is, there needs to be a continued deepening of mutual legal assistance channel bilaterally and multilaterally.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This may involve a memorandum of understanding between authorities and their counterparts abroad on things like digital evidence requests, standard operating timelines, as well as having dedicated offices to oversee and expedite such cross-border coordination and collaboration.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My last point, beyond strengthening our laws against scammers, we must continue to build a scam-resilient society.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is because the law cannot carry full load.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We have to build habits, skills, systems that help Singaporeans to determine scams early and act fast.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We want a vigilant public not a fearful one.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore must never become a place that we suspect every single message and live in constant anxiety.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Pause, check, then decide when encountering something suspicious.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, we should consider incorporating more practical scam education within our schools and community to enable our ability to detect scam activities.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, as scams continue to evolve, we must continue to do more to educate or being able to identify deepfakes.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We have made progress through Police Anti-Scam Command ScamShield, but I think we can go further.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Just as from time to time at work, we have to take cybersecurity quizzes, I wonder if we can have scam quizzes built into ScamShield.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And perhaps users who complete the quizzes could also earn some reward or incentive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, if you can get 20 or 30 questions right, a pretty high bar, it could entail you to have additional Community Development Council vouchers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The goal, it is really just to be more scam resilient.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Speak to scam victims, you know that often times they feel shame and fear, viewed as silly or naive by their loved ones or others or even being blamed for their own troubles.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, many may choose to stay silent and not even report being scammed; and scammers will rejoice in their silence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, we must, hence, fight this stigma, make early help the norm.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Just one reference number, find the details all there.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Giving scam victims discretion and privacy is equally important as well, including ensuring private spaces for conversations and the option to bring someone else along.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We should also consider inviting those who wish to step forward to tell their stories in a safe and respectful setting.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because I have learned that sharing stories is powerful, because then survivors choose to share, even anonymously, they show others it is okay to seek help.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It reduces the shame that keeps many silent and turn painful experiences into lessons that protect and empower others.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is how we stay vigilant without becoming fearful, keep trust alive while protecting one another.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Swift in catching offenders, certain in delivering justice and smart in building public awareness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because at the end of day, the best deterrence is not fear of punishment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is a society that is alert, resilient and one step ahead of scammers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I read with great concern about the recent media coverage of Singaporeans being involved in scam syndicate operations in Cambodia.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In one of the reported cases, a Singaporean was alleged to be the leader of the crime ring, targeting Singaporeans in government impersonation scams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Their use of the Singaporean accent was meant to reassure the victims that the calls were genuine.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Scams are a major source of crime in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, we are far more likely to get scammed online than to be robbed in the streets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These figures are a representation that scam cases continue to plague our country.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When I first joined the Police in 1995, cheating cases were common but limited largely to face-to-face interactions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Over time, as Singapore's digital penetration grew, scam archetypes evolved to love scams on WeChat to the current situation, where so many variants of scams affect different segments of our population.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Bill's proposal to introduce mandatory caning for offenders of scams is, therefore, highly welcomed and timely, as we need to send a clear signal that our legal system has no tolerance for those who scam and prey on others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, when it comes to enforcement, it is often the most vulnerable who are recruited as mules, who are caught.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Syndicate bosses are often based offshore and it can be tough for our local law enforcement to take them to task.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask how the SPF are working with the foreign enforcement agencies, including with Interpol and member agencies of the Anti-Money Laundering Case Coordination and Collaboration Network (AC3N) to take these criminal masterminds to task.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For offences with proposed discretionary caning, such as those involving individuals who launder scam proceeds, supply SIM cards or provide Singpass credentials, I would like to ask whether sentencing guidelines will be made available to the Courts and, if so, what would these sentencing guidelines be?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would vulnerable offenders, such as youths and those with mild intellectual disabilities, be given greater leniency if they are preyed upon and roped into scam operations?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How can we do more to protect these vulnerable individuals from being taken advantage of by the scam syndicates?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Ticket scams pertaining to live entertainment events have been a growing concern for the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Consumers tell us that ticket scams are a particular area of concern as many event goers try to get tickets to A-list events at all costs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many of them simply cannot buy tickets on the primary market due to the presence of bots.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They try all means possible to attend the events by their favourite artiste, even at the risk of purchasing fake tickets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Members would recall reading news articles about ticket scams whenever an A-list event takes place in Singapore, from Taylor Swift to Coldplay to Andy Lau.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Taylor Swift Eras Tour concert that was held in Singapore in March 2024, became an unfortunate incident where many locals and international consumers became scam victims.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Consumer Protection Review Panel, which I co-chair, is looking into this issue deeply.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: For example, the Panel is actively engaging ticket service platforms to explore establishing authorised ticket sales platforms to provide consumers with greater certainty that tickets resold on proper platforms are legitimate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Other suggestions, include phasing out paper tickets and to only have digital tickets with dynamic QR codes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But while the industry players and CASE do our best to tackle the issue, we cannot succeed in eradicating the problem of ticket scams without support from the Government.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Because if left unaddressed, these scams could threaten to derail Singapore's efforts to anchor ourselves as the region's entertainment hub.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In closing, the amendments proposed under the Bill are timely, as it will send a strong signal that tackling scams continue to be a national priority.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must continue to act firmly against scam syndicates, while having a care on how we treat vulnerable citizens who are roped into scam operations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also urge the Ministry to also look into how we can deal with ticketing scams more decisively, as it affects a large number of consumers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is an understatement today that scams are the scourge of societies.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, to put this into perspective, this averages out to be about more than 120 of such cases each day, more than five cases an hour.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In terms of losses, an average of $2.5 million lost each day to scams.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These figures are astonishing to say the least.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, the monies lost to scams are not representative of the entire cost of such criminal enterprises for society because if we tabulate the man-hours and other valuable resources deployed to combat scams, then the total amount would be many times that, just the loss quantum.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The motivation of scammers is clear, their ill-gotten rewards are enormous, vis-à-vis the risks.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: All these, at the expense of their victims.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe all of us have met scam victims at our meet-the-people sessions and have heard their pleas for help, as many Members have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is heartbreaking to hear of Singaporeans having their honest and hard-earned monies despicably stolen from them.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, just two weeks ago, a family member of mine almost fell victim to one such scam.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I do not know whether the scammer knew that I was going to make a speech in Parliament so soon.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, she received a call from someone claiming to be a Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) officer, who told her that her bank account had been compromised for illegal transactions and then, assured her that he would help her to resolve the issue.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: He then told her to lock herself in the room as he guided her through the process via video call and he told her many times not to let anyone know in the family.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, flustered and helpless, my family member ended up spending several hours on the call with this scammer.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And in this time, she set up a crypto-currency account, she has never learned about crypto before.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She terminated an investment savings account and transferred the funds from the investment savings account to her savings account.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But fortunately for her, she informed my wife after the call, who then informed me and we were able to stop any losses in time.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But this is a very common modus operandi of scammers now.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
