text: They get into the minds of their victims by first sending them into a panic mode and then, assure them that they can help by impersonating themselves as public officials.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And I told my family member: I said when they told you to lock yourself in a room and not tell anyone, alarm bells should have started ringing in your head!

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But she told me that during the entire process she was almost in a trance-like state.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I think similar to what some of the other Members have shared.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, my family member was fortunate to have family members around.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I worry very much for my residents who are seniors, who stay alone and I have also met residents who are even younger than me all preyed to the similar tactics that I have just shared.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, no condemnation leveled against scams and scammers to me would be considered unjust.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And clearly, the existing sanctions are not adequate and do not effectively deter scammers and potential scammers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, it is, therefore, timely that this Bill seeks to enhance the penalties for scams offences.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With this as context, I would like to raise several points and clarifications for the Senior Minister of State's response.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, clause 63 of the Bill inserts a new section 416B in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this new section, with respect to the element of deceit by way of remote communications, the operative threshold is "mainly", mainly via digital or remote means.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But in this current day and age, almost all our daily communications are arguably "mainly" done through digital and remote means, whether it is emails, social media, text messaging.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, I want to find out what is the rationale for this statutory requirement and how should the word "mainly" be legally interpreted?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, the Bill introduces "mandatory" and "discretionary" caning.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Recently, in The Straits Times, 17 July 2025, 15 people were reportedly being investigated for sharing their Singpass credentials, some used to open bank accounts and register for mobile phone lines for scam purposes.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the weekend, CNA also reported that the Police had arrested 38 people acting as money mules for scammers, having sold or rented their YouTrip accounts for monetary gains.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because Mr Speaker, scammers, members and recruiters of scam syndicates and the scam mules, all these participants are essential to the operations of the scam enterprise.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, what is the rationale for such a distinction between caning to be meted out to these various players in the ecosystem?

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The impersonation of government officials is probably the most deplorable of the various types of scams we have discussed today because it carries the very real danger of also undermining the public's confidence in the Government and the integrity and security of our services.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have all heard feedback that in a bid to avoid scammers, many Singaporeans have chosen either not to answer any calls from unknown or private numbers.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When they receive SMS-es that are sent by official sources, they read it with apprehension and suspicion.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, the fear of being scammed has affected us all.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, we should do the same now for scams and if we are similarly successful as we were or we are with vandalism, we can review this in the future as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We enact harsh laws but not after deep and careful consideration to protect the everyday Singaporean – honest, hardworking, resilient and really just doing his or her best for their families.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, Mr Speaker, notwithstanding my clarifications, I support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This aligns with Singapore's history of strengthening laws against trends in crime.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support the Bill but seek clarification firstly on complementary social and support measures to tackle the scourge of scams between deterrence and dialogue.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Bill distinguishes money mules from scam syndicate leaders, introducing mandatory caning for scammers and discretionary caning for money mules.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This toughens measures against scams, addressing a national issue.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But beyond financial figures, victims have experienced ruined family relationships, depression and some even turned to suicide.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Caning is, therefore, an effective deterrent in reducing loan shark harassment, but I have two clarifications on this.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First is for those above 50 years old where caning is unsuitable, how will alternative penalties be applied?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And whether these enhanced penalties will immediately apply to the 27 Singaporeans allegedly found to be part of the Cambodian scam syndicate, if found guilty?

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While the Bill assigns lower culpability to money mules, their punishment is still significant.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support the new offences but suggest new ways to augment the effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As criminal lawyers note, deterrence is not the only crime control method; focusing solely on increased penalties might ignore root issues.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mules might be financially disadvantaged, incentivised by financial hardship to sell Singpass details or personal access.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A worrying trend involves youths becoming scam mules; and a misconception that only elderly are victims when those in the 21 to 59 age group, who might be digitally native and overconfident, thereby constituting most victims.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Greater deterrence therefore may not address economic hardship or coercion, but our approach needs to be balanced, focusing on financial literacy and legitimate employment.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Given the heavy penalties for potential money mules, public education on offence severity is needed, especially demographics of those less aware.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must also incorporate these messaging, using technology, like the ScamShield app, a powerful intelligence network against scam trends.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another suggestion includes encouraging money mules to become informants, aligning with Government efforts against local scam enablers, where those actively cooperating with authorities by providing information on scam operations could receive reduced sentencing.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But often the investigation of potential money mules might be complex and lengthy.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is hard to distinguish those who participate as a mule versus those whose personal information might have been misused and compromised.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During investigation, these individuals might face strict restrictions, including frozen bank accounts, affected credit ratings, making it hard to receive salaries, to pay bills or to receive Government benefits.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, I will speak about strengthening protections for vulnerable victims against abuse.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This tool ensures penalties for the "worst of the worst" egregious cases.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite serious penalties for abuse, advocates for vulnerable groups, like domestic helpers, highlight root causes lie in power disparity and victims' fear-driven difficulty in seeking help, sometimes due to social isolation.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Increased abuse penalties also need to come with complementary protection and empowerment for potential victims, especially for early intervention.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Existing support measures can be expanded through awareness of help avenues and increased checks on these foreign domestic workers.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Enhanced penalties also apply to abuse of children under 14 and vulnerable persons.

speaker: Mr Cai Yinzhou (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Beyond age, if I may suggest stipulating definitions of vulnerable persons for seniors or even those with disabilities using metrics, like the Activities of Daily Living score, which is an established tool for measuring functional ability.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The nature of crime is rapidly changing and I am glad the Government is taking steps to update our laws to keep pace.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The legislative amendments protect our people both by enhancing deterrence and ensuring that, where deterrence is met with recalcitrance, the offenders receive rehabilitation and a chance to mend their ways.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In supporting this Bill, I would like to expand upon two areas for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: First, the reach of penalties for scam-related offences.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In chess, the king is the most important piece, it can determine victory or defeat and is the most strategic centre of the game.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Like the chess king, the kingpin is crucial to the overall strategy.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The kingpin is the one that defines the game.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new penalties currently apply to three categories of offenders.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: First, those who perpetrate scams or other forms of cheating; those who are members of or recruit members for scam syndicates; and those who facilitate the scams, such as through mule activities, by supplying the scammers with bank accounts, Singpass accounts and SIM cards.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These persons who should be charged with these penalties are likely to be low-level operatives.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While this would improve deterrence and disrupt scam networks, we would not be rid of scams until we apprehend the principals and the financiers, and demolish scam networks entirely.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Scams today, are intricate supply chains, which include clearly defined functions of data acquisition, scripting, operations and even technology.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The key to sustaining such operations are the key decision makers, in other words, the kingpin, to put the supply chain together.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: For a solution to be sustainable, it must lower the incentive for scammers by cancelling out the profitability.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Scams have grown increasingly sophisticated and transnational, exploiting digital platforms and encrypted communication channels that make enforcement challenging.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How are we handling the transnational nature of scam offences?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While local laws have their place, many cyber-enabled scams cross international boundaries such that the lines in jurisdictions are blurred.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Scam centres are based in other countries, such as Cambodia and Myanmar, but their victims are our Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Criminal Law (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill apply or are we using our diplomatic channels to motivate enforcement?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Are we able to send the SPF to those countries to provide support or technical assistance?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Why were these links not discovered by us earlier?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What action is our Government taking and are there checks being done to ensure no other Singaporeans are implicated?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: There may also be a need to implement sufficient safeguards for persons based in Singapore vis-à-vis foreign law risks.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the legal aspect, the importance of public education cannot be understated as each individual is his/her own first line of defence against scams.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How can we detect and respond more quickly to new modalities of scams?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: How do we then shorten the time and respond quicker between detection and public education efforts?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: What plans are in place to monitor the impact of current outreach and education efforts and to increase their effectiveness amid the evolving nature of scams?

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: On the flipside, it is critical that these measures avoid a chilling effect, whereby people cross the threshold from reasonable caution to pervasive distrust of all online activity, even the legitimate ones.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: In this ever-evolving digital world, we must empower our people to be prudent without pulling back unnecessarily.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, security measures should be carefully assessed before implementation to ensure that they do not make legitimate online processes unjustifiably onerous for users.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Second, our approach to exclude caning penalties based on age.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, Singapore's maximum age for caning is 50 years old.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Our average health-span, defined as years of good health, is now at 75, as shared by the Prime Minister, at the National Day Rally.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: Revising the caning age limit upwards would align with the trend towards an ageing society whereby, assuming status quo in crime rates, the average age of offenders is expected to increase year on year.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This ensures that deterrence stays relevant and effective even as the age profile of our population changes.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This also avoids situations that may seem unjust where offenders may be spared simply because they are caught and sentenced after they pass the age of 50.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: It strengthens the deterrent effect of penalties whilst simultaneously ensuring that offenders have opportunities for rehabilitation, achieving both objectives.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: The new penalties target scam perpetrators, gang members and recruiters, as well as those who provide SIM cards or Singpass credentials to criminals.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These individuals may not hold high positions within scam syndicates.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: As the saying goes, "to catch bandits, first catch their leader." I hope the Minister can clarify whether, from a more comprehensive perspective, the new penalties are also targeting the masterminds behind criminal syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Joan Pereira highlighted bullying cases which involve the distribution of intimate images of minors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We agree that a firm stance should be taken against such acts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I also thank Ms Pereira for her suggestions regarding upstream preventive measures and downstream victim support and agree that these are important to complement the proposals in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Measures have, indeed, been put in place to help victims of sexual offences, including minors, through the criminal justice process.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan suggested introducing discretionary caning for administrators of online locations circulating obscene material.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) will continue to monitor the situation and assess if there is a need to review the penalties further.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Next, on the enhanced penalties for fatal abuse of vulnerable victims.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou highlighted that beyond increasing the penalties for abuse of vulnerable victims, it is also important to have upstream preventive measures.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such measures have been put in place by the Ministry of Social and Family Development and Ministry of Manpower.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai also suggested including seniors and persons with disabilities within the definition of vulnerable persons.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Under our current laws, a "vulnerable person" refers to those who, due to mental or physical infirmity, disability or incapacity, are substantially unable to protect themselves from abuse, neglect or self-neglect.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Seniors and persons with disabilities who meet this definition will be protected by the enhanced penalties we propose to impose on their abusers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: On the new offence to criminalise the doxxing of a public servant, Dr Wan Rizal asked if offenders could escape liability by claiming that the falsehood was minor or was disguised in humour or sarcasm.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Courts apply an objective standard in determining what constitutes a false statement of fact and will not take such claims at face value.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal sought to clarify when agencies would use levers under POFMA versus the new offence of doxxing accompanied by a falsehood.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The POFMA levers focus on the likely impact of the false statement of fact on key public interests, such as Singapore's security, public health, safety, tranquillity or finances, or public confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: On the other hand, the new offence is targeted at protecting public servants and thus, requires that the false statement of fact relate to the public servant.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Different cases may require one lever or the other, or even a combination of the two.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such a determination would have to be made on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal and Ms Sylvia Lim had questions regarding the scope of the new offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked if the new offence would extend to public service workers who perform public duties, but are not public servants.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The new offence will only cover public servants.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: False statements against public servants can directly undermine confidence in our public institutions and so, warrant a higher penalty.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, doxxing of a public service worker is already an offence under POHA that carries enhanced penalties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lim asked if the new offence would extend to politicians, such as Ministers and MPs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To be clear, persons who harass MPs are nonetheless still liable for an offence under POHA, or other offences, like criminal intimidation and criminal defamation, depending on the facts of the case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lim asked if the definition of a "related person" of a public servant could be made more precise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A "related person" of a public servant is defined as a person whose safety or well-being the public servant would reasonably be expected to be seriously concerned about.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The rationale for extending the offence to cover doxxing of "related persons" of a public servant is because offenders may target persons close to a public servant to get to the public servant.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The question of whether a person falls within the definition of a "related person" is an objective one that the Courts will determine based on the facts of the case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The concept of a "related person" is not new and already exists within POHA.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the placement of the illustration in the Explanatory Note instead of within the provision.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We assess that the provision is clear enough.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Not all offence provisions need to have illustrations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In any case, the Explanatory Note is available in the public domain and can be referred to by all stakeholders, including Counsel and the Courts, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Comments from Members are largely divided into three categories: the Government's general anti-scam measures, adequacy of the proposed penalties and clarifications on the proposals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying asked about the Government's plans to implement more robust industry safeguards to disrupt the communication channels used by scam syndicates to approach victims.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To address this, the Government has worked with online platforms to implement anti-scam safeguards and remove scam-tainted content and accounts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government will consider further legislative levers as necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Given the transnational nature of scams, Mr David Hoe asked if Singapore can establish a permanent joint disruption cell bringing together both governments and private entities in different jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Lee Hui Ying asked if Singapore takes action against overseas scam syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I agree with Mr Hoe, Mr Yong and Ms Lee that it is critical for governments to work together to disrupt scams and recover assets.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: FRONTIER+ now covers 13 jurisdictions, including Hong Kong, the Republic of Korea, Malaysia and Thailand.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are actively encouraging other jurisdictions to join FRONTIER+.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Hoe also asked if the Ministry publishes regular updates on the number of scammers caught and their penalties, for deterrence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: SPF regularly publishes its enforcement efforts through press releases following key operations, and via the biannual Scams and Cybercrime Briefs.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Police also arrested 93 persons and investigated another 119 persons for their suspected involvement in providing fraudulently registered SIM cards for monetary gain.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The message is clear – if you enable scams, even indirectly, you will face the full force of the law.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yong asked if we could do more to prevent vulnerable individuals, such as youths, from becoming scam mules.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government has been running many public education initiatives to educate youths about the consequences of facilitating scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For example, MHA has worked with MOE to conduct school talks and insert anti-scam messaging into advisories, which are disseminated to students in primary and secondary schools, as well as Institutes of Higher Learning.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Hoe asked if more could be done to support scam victims and encourage them to come forward and make reports.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Police have developed a resource guide on what victims should do and the community support that they can seek.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The guide is available in all four official languages and has been delivered to all households, with online copies available on the SPF and ScamShield websites.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where necessary, the Police may also refer victims to a Victim Care Officer for psychological first aid and crisis intervention.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Hoe also highlighted the need to build a resilient public, and suggested gamification and making scam quizzes more accessible.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I agree with him that we should consider new and creative ways to get the message across.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I hope businesses too will consider these ideas and proactively help shore up their employees' digital defence against online threats including scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lee also asked about the Government's efforts to monitor the effectiveness of anti-scam public education tools.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: SPF periodically commissions surveys on the outreach and engagement performance of the Government's scam education initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yong also asked if the Government would consider introducing anti-ticketing scam laws to tackle concert ticket scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Over the past year, MHA and the Police have worked with secondary resale platforms, like Carousell and Facebook Marketplace, to disallow listings of resale tickets for high-demand concerts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA is also working with the Ministry of Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, and Singapore Tourism Board (STB) to explore other measures to address concert ticket scams, including the establishment of authorised ticket resale platforms and consumer education campaigns.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai Yinzhou highlighted that stiffer penalties alone will not be effective in dealing with the scams problem.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked if the Government had considered other measures outside the criminal law to disrupt scam syndicates.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government adopts a whole-of-society approach to deal with scams, ranging from upstream measures to prevent scammers from approaching victims to the usage of technology to scale up disruption efforts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Members may wish to refer to the Mid-Year Scams and Cybercrime brief published by the SPF for an overview of these measures.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, on the adequacy of the proposed penalties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Hoe asked if we relied on any benchmark in deciding the maximum number of strokes for scam-related offenders and if a ceiling of 12 strokes provides sufficient deterrence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In deciding the maximum number of strokes, the Ministry considered factors including the existing penalty regime for offences of a similar nature, such as unlicensed moneylending.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We assess that 12 strokes is sufficient for now but will monitor the situation closely.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Courts will have discretion to decide the actual number of strokes, and will take into account the principle of proportionality that Mr Hoe talked about.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Foo Cexiang asked if caning should be made mandatory for scam mules as well given that mules are essential to the scam enterprise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Foo also asked if caning should be mandatory for scam-related offenders with a nexus to government official impersonation scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan suggested for the penalties for scams and scam-related offences to be increased and aligned with drug offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Scammers indeed rely heavily on the enablers provided by scam mules to deceive victims and profit from their scams.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dismantling this local ecosystem of enablers is essential to addressing the scams situation.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Notwithstanding the need to deter scam mules, MHA recognises the need to be calibrated in our approach.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA will monitor the situation and adjust the penalties further if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi and Mr Cai asked if leniency could be shown for mules who step forward as informants.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: An offender's degree of cooperation with the authorities and degree of remorse are already mitigating factors that the Courts may consider.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai made the point that scam mules are often from vulnerable backgrounds and are incentivised to facilitate scams because of financial hardships.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Perhaps, he has seen a recent The Straits Times article on crime gangs quoting an expert drawing connections between economic inequality and family-linked crime.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government has many measures in place to uplift and support families and individuals in financial need.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA's view on this matter, therefore, is that financial hardship cannot be used as a justification to facilitate or commit scams, or any crime for that matter.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And as many Members have pointed out, scams are not victimless crimes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The victims can suffer permanent, irreparable harm, not just financial harm, but also severe psychological and in some cases, physical harm.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To reduce such harm, we must be prepared to deter potential scam mules with sufficiently stiff penalties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked if there would be sentencing guidance to clearly define the key roles in a scam to aid the Courts in distinguishing between the masterminds and low-level participants.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yong asked if the sentencing guidelines would accord leniency for youths and those with intellectual disabilities.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, the various scam-related offences already differentiate penalties based on the fault element.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In general, the higher the level of culpability, the higher the maximum penalty for that offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where an offender has been charged for a particular offence, the legal burden will be on the Public Prosecutor to prove that all the elements of the offence, including the fault element, have been met.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In sentencing, the Courts will consider all the facts and circumstances of the case, including mitigating factors, such as the offender's young age or intellectual capabilities.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal also asked if there was a checklist defining what counts as reasonable steps that an individual can take to ensure that an enabler would not be used to commit or to facilitate the commission of a scam.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It would not be practical to provide an exhaustive checklist.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It will be for the Courts to decide whether the steps taken, if any, meet the legal threshold, based on the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, all individuals should protect their Singpass credentials, payment accounts and SIM cards, and should not provide them to unknown individuals no matter what the unknown individuals claim they would be used for.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai asked if the enhanced penalties can apply retrospectively to the 27 Singaporeans who are alleged to be part of the scam syndicate in Cambodia, if found guilty.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Foo asked about the need to scope scam offences to deceit mainly by way of remote communication.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A defining characteristic of scams is the substantial use of remote communications to reach and engage victims.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Using remote communication allows scammers to significantly scale up their operations and frustrate law enforcement efforts by allowing them to reach victims without entering Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: They can, therefore, be far more insidious than traditional cheating cases and warrant the application of the enhanced penalties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have been careful in the choice of words; in particular, we have chosen not to scope scam offences to deceit only by way of remote communication, as we cannot rule out the possibility of scammers making some form of physical outreach to victims as part of their modus operandi.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such scammers should not escape liability for caning because of this technicality.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It will be for the Courts to decide whether each case meets the definition of scams as set out in law.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lim asked what led MHA to decide on tightening the penalties for scam and scam-related offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA periodically reviews the adequacy of our criminal penalties.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Fadli suggested using recovered funds to finance scam victim restitution fund.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, there are significant difficulties with returning recovered assets through a restitution fund, and any such approach has to be carefully considered, as Mr Fadli himself has also pointed out.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Lastly, there were also some comments from Members that go beyond the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lee raised the ongoing case involving Prince Holding Group.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As this is beyond the scope of the Bill, I invite Ms Lee to file a separate Parliamentary Question with her detailed questions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: But I will say that this case demonstrates the Police's ability to advance investigations against highly complex, large-scale transnational criminal networks.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will continue to work with our foreign law enforcement counterparts and financial intelligence units, as well as leverage domestic coordination platforms like the AC3N, which Mr Yong had earlier highlighted, to act against such organised crime groups and money laundering networks.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lim asked if the Extradition Act can be used in future to transfer suspects from foreign jurisdictions to Singapore and whether joint operations with foreign jurisdictions would occur more frequently.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The syndicates must know that they cannot take refuge anywhere.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The law will eventually catch up with them.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Cai asked about the application of caning to offenders who are above 50 years old.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And Ms Lee also suggested reviewing the maximum age limit for caning.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Government has previously explained that we do not intend to do so.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, the number of men above the age of 50 at the point of arrest for serious offences that attract the punishment of caning is significantly lower than that for men aged 50 years and younger.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Henry Kwek suggested the adoption of an age-sensitive charging approach for younger offenders.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Cases involving offenders below the age of 16 will generally continue to be heard in the Youth Court.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Even for such offenders, I would highlight that the prosecution retains discretion in deciding on the appropriate charge and whether to apply for these cases to be transmitted out of the Youth Court.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In exercising this discretion, the Public Prosecutor will consider the full facts and circumstances of the case including the age of the offender.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The proposed amendments enhance our efforts to maintain a safe and secure Singapore and I thank Members for their support.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there clarifications for the Senior Minister of State Ms Sylvia Lim?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have one clarification for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For the recent joint operation with Cambodia in September which I mentioned in my speech, it was not mentioned that it is under FRONTIER+.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, does this mean that Cambodia has actually not signed on to FRONTIER+?

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: So, even as we expand networks with different jurisdictions, it also does not prevent us from working bilaterally with them.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications for the Senior Minister of State?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 3.52 pm until 4.10 pm.
